stem: A 74-year-old woman is reviewed for long-standing type 2 diabetes and hypertension, both poorly controlled. She has a 5-year history of kidney disease with growing protein loss in the urine and a creatinine clearance now down to 30 mL/min. Her pressure today is 165/95 mm Hg, and she has leg edema. Heart and lung examinations are normal.
oneliner: 74F + T2DM + HTN + 5 y kidney disease + proteinuria + CrCl 30 + leg edema → expected labs vs healthy?
ask: Compared with a healthy person, which set of findings is most likely?

whyNot.A: Failing kidneys make **less** erythropoietin and calcitriol, so neither hematocrit nor calcitriol goes up
whyNot.B: PTH and calcitriol fit, but **CrCl of 30** with years of disease means the kidney's erythropoietin output is also down, so hematocrit falls
whyNot.D: PTH is **raised** by low calcitriol and phosphate retention, not lowered
whyNot.E: With **CrCl 30**, the kidney's hormone jobs are impaired, so nothing stays normal

why: Damaged renal tissue makes **less erythropoietin**, so hematocrit falls, and has **less 1-alpha-hydroxylase**, so calcitriol falls. Low calcitriol and phosphate retention lower serum calcium, which drives **secondary hyperparathyroidism**.

idea.rule: Kidney failure means low EPO, low calcitriol and high PTH.
also: Lupus nephritis progressing to chronic kidney disease

stem: A 61-year-old man with hypertension starts a new loop diuretic and has labs and a volume assessment after 3 days.
oneliner: 61M + HTN + new loop diuretic × 3 days → plasma volume, bicarbonate, pH?
ask: Which set of changes is most likely?

options.A: Plasma volume ↑, serum bicarbonate ↓, arterial pH ↓
options.B: Plasma volume ↓, serum bicarbonate ↓, arterial pH ↓
options.C: Plasma volume ↔, serum bicarbonate ↑, arterial pH ↑
options.D: Plasma volume ↓, serum bicarbonate ↑, arterial pH ↑
options.E: Plasma volume ↑, serum bicarbonate ↑, arterial pH ↑

whyNot.A: A diuretic makes him **lose** fluid, so plasma volume does not rise
whyNot.B: Volume is lost, but a loop diuretic does not cause an **acidosis**
whyNot.C: **Three days** of a loop diuretic leaves a net salt and water deficit, so plasma volume does not stay normal
whyNot.E: Alkalosis is right, but the **diuresis** shrinks, not expands, plasma volume

answer: Plasma volume ↓, serum bicarbonate ↑, arterial pH ↑ (contraction alkalosis)
why: Blocking the **Na-K-2Cl cotransporter** causes salt and water loss, so plasma volume falls. The volume loss activates **RAAS**, and aldosterone drives H+ secretion and bicarbonate reabsorption; a smaller extracellular volume also concentrates bicarbonate. The result is **contraction alkalosis**.
chain: Loop blocked in thick ascending limb
Salt and water lost: plasma volume falls
More distal H+ secretion, more HCO3 reabsorbed

idea.rule: Salt and chloride loss that shrinks the ECF, with aldosterone switched on, gives contraction alkalosis.
also: Cystic fibrosis with heavy sweat chloride loss

stem: An 18-month-old girl is brought in for poor growth and constant wet diapers. Her weight and length both sit at the 3rd percentile; she is dehydrated and floppy, and has bowed legs. A slit-lamp examination shows crystals in both corneas. Serum shows low phosphate and low potassium, and a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Urine pH is 5, with glucose, phosphate and amino acids all present in the urine.
oneliner: 18mo F + poor growth + polyuria + bowed legs + corneal crystals + low K, low phosphate + normal-gap acidosis + urine pH 5 + glucosuria, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria → what causes the acidosis?
ask: Which mechanism best explains her acidosis?

options.A: Failure of H+ secretion by distal intercalated cells
options.B: Reduced bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule
options.C: Aldosterone resistance in the collecting duct
options.D: Excess lactic acid production by tissues
options.E: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition in the distal tubule

whyNot.A: Distal H+ failure cannot acidify urine; hers is **pH 5**, so distal acidification works
whyNot.C: Aldosterone resistance causes **high potassium**; hers is **low**
whyNot.D: Lactate adds unmeasured anions and widens the gap; hers is a **normal gap**
whyNot.E: A distal block would leave **urine pH high**, and she has **glucose and amino acid losses** that point proximal

answer: Reduced proximal bicarbonate reabsorption (renal Fanconi syndrome)
why: Glucose, phosphate, amino acids and bicarbonate are all reabsorbed in the **proximal tubule**, so losing all of them together means a global proximal defect (**Fanconi syndrome**; **corneal crystals** suggest cystinosis). Bicarbonate wasting causes a **normal-gap acidosis**, and the intact distal nephron can still acidify urine to pH 5.
chain: Cystine builds up in proximal tubule cells
Glucose, phosphate, amino acids and bicarbonate are lost
Serum bicarbonate falls with a normal anion gap

idea.rule: Several solutes lost together in the urine means a proximal tubule defect.
